papers.title: Emergence and Collapse of Leader-Follower Flocks through Phantom Targets: Surprise Nullification in Bayesian and Inverse Bayesian Inference
papers.abstract: In Bayesian and inverse Bayesian (BIB) inference, a large prediction error can trigger surprise nullification, which expands belief and likelihood variances by a common factor, leaving the updated variance ratio the same as in standard Bayesian updating. This can increase belief uncertainty while keeping the learning rate low. In the simulations, three agents used BIB inference to predict one another's positions and moved toward those predictions, repeatedly forming leader-follower flocks that subsequently collapsed despite having no alignment rules or designated leaders. Three leadership criteria (front position, heading stability, and flock initiation) identified the same agent in 89% of eligible flocks, with different agents serving as leaders across flocks. Flocks formed when an agent nearly stopped incorporating another's observations (link cut) and moved straight toward a predicted position detached from reality (phantom target), thereby attracting followers. Link cuts arose when two successive resets assigned a very small and then an ordinary likelihood variance, sharply increasing the likelihood-to-belief variance ratio. Flocks collapsed upon link recovery or when returning phantom targets balanced the leader's forward and backward attractions. Without nullification, cuts persisted throughout the analysis period; expanding only belief variance caused recovery within a few steps. Expanding likelihood variance as well allowed cuts to persist while belief uncertainty grew, enabling later resets and recovery. Thus, nullification preserves relative precision, allowing cuts and flocks to persist, while reducing absolute precision to enable recovery and collapse, reconciling these seemingly opposing processes through a single operation. These results suggest that, in this model, individually inaccurate predictions can give rise to collective order.

papers.title: Flocking Time and Graph Volume in Nonlinear Cucker-Smale Models with Dynamic Networks
papers.abstract: This study proposes a Cucker-Smale model incorporating dynamic networks and the discrete $p$-Laplacian ($p \in (1,2)$) and analyzes the relationship between flocking time constraints and graph connectivity from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. We establish that this model achieves flocking within finite time and derive a quantitative relationship between the lower bound of flocking time and graph volume. Based on these results, we observe that imposing sufficiently small flocking time induces an increase in network volume, and that larger initial velocity variance requires greater volume under the same time constraint. In our experiments, we trained a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each time step. Under the most stringent time constraint, the maximum average number of connections increased sharply, confirming a threshold effect. The negative correlation between convergence time and average number of connections reflects the theoretical results well. This study provides quantitative evidence for the phenomenon that time constraints induce connection mobilization.

papers.title: Dynamics-preserving graph sparsification
papers.abstract: Many dynamical systems unfold on networks of nodes coupled by edge interactions. This work is motivated by the following question: can we remove most edges from a networked dynamical system without significantly altering its behavior? For a given network, our goal is to find a sparser network that approximately preserves the dynamics on the nodes. We first study linear diffusion, where node values evolve according to the graph Laplacian. The dominant network sparsification method, effective resistance sampling, preserves all Laplacian eigenvalues within a uniform multiplicative bound. We show that with a limited edge budget, this is dynamically inefficient: diffusion is dominated by the slowest-decaying modes, so enforcing a uniform guarantee spends edges on fast modes that barely affect long-term dynamics. Based on this observation, we derive Diffusion Spectral Error (DSE), which evaluates in closed form the typical error in trajectories between the original and sparsified graphs over random initial conditions. Minimizing this error, which naturally prioritizes slow modes, yields sparse networks explicitly designed to preserve dynamics. At the same sparsification levels, DSE sparsification often preserves diffusion dynamics with several-fold lower error than effective resistance sampling, and up to two orders of magnitude lower on strongly modular networks. Although derived in a linear context, we empirically find that DSE sparsification gives similar improvements in the Kuramoto model (a nonlinear system of coupled oscillators), where DSE sparsification approximately preserves the synchronization threshold and, at strong coupling, order-parameter trajectories.

papers.title: Why do continual physical learners need sleep?
papers.abstract: Sleep is widespread across the animal kingdom, including in organisms without a centralized nervous system. Does learning create a need for sleep, even without biology? To explore this question, we study a disordered spring network trained to perform a sequence of mechanical allosteric tasks through local changes in bond stiffness. We find that continual learning progressively reduces the network's ability to acquire new tasks as individual bonds become increasingly specialized. We identify an exact algebraic relationship between the polarization of bond dominance and the network's remaining learning capacity, providing a quantitative measure of this loss of adaptability. We then demonstrate that random internal perturbations allow individual bonds to estimate their mechanical dominance and locally adjust their stiffnesses to restore learning capacity. However, the forces associated with active learning bias these local measurements and interfere with restoration. Separating learning and repair into wake-like and sleep-like phases removes this interference and improves continual-learning performance. Our results suggest that the need for offline restorative phases can emerge from the mechanics of physical learning, even in systems without biological components.

papers.title: Gradual emergence of temporal structures depending on the distance between neighboring callers in natural habitat of male treefrogs
papers.abstract: Collective behavior, such as in-phase and anti-phase synchronizations in acoustic animals, is one of the most striking examples of self-organization in animal communication. However, understanding how synchronization emerges in natural environments has been limited by the difficulty of tracking multiple callers simultaneously in the wild. Here, we quantified spatio-temporal frequency characteristics in the choruses of wild treefrogs by combining large-scale sound-imaging and microphone-array systems. First, we performed field recordings by combining the sound-imaging system (25-66 units of sound-imaging devices) and microphone-array system (16-24 channels of microphones) between 2021 and 2023. Second, we analyzed the video and audio data and quantified the call frequency, call timing, and caller position of each male across 11 choruses comprising 66 males in total. Based on this dataset, we have shown that synchronized behavior gradually emerges between neighboring callers depending on their distances even when the call frequency and chorus density moderately vary. These findings provide field-based evidence for how local acoustic interactions generate collective temporal order in animal groups.
